The Company has engaged KFin as the agency for providing the e-voting facility.

The Company is providing the facility of remote e-voting and e-voting during the AGM to its Members in respect of all the resolutions set forth in the Notice of the AGM. The Notice, inter alia, contains detailed instructions for remote e-voting, attending the AGM through VC/OAVM and registration of e-mail addresses by the Members. Members holding shares as on Friday, September 11, 2026, (“Cut-off date”), shall be entitled to cast their votes electronically on the resolutions set out in the Notice of the AGM. The remote e-voting shall commence from 9:00 A.M. (IST) on Sunday, September 13, 2026, and shall remain open till 5:00 P.M. (IST) on Thursday, September 17, 2026. We pioneered a zero-commission model that enables sellers to participate in e-commerce without the commission structures traditionally charged by online marketplaces. Combined with low-cost order fulfilment, this makes Meesho one of the most economical platforms to sell on in India and lowers the barriers to entrepreneurship for businesses of all sizes.

Our active seller base grew 87.0% YoY to 961k in FY26, reflecting the increasing attractiveness of Meesho as a platform for entrepreneurs across India. Our logistics ecosystem comprises first and last mile delivery partners, sorting centres, truck operators, and end-to-end logistics providers. As order volumes on the platform continue to grow, logistics partners benefit from access to a large and expanding pool of e-commerce demand across India.
Orders on Meesho are fulfilled either through Valmo, our proprietary technology platform that orchestrates fulfilment across a multi-partner logistics network, or directly through end-to-end logistics partners. In turn, creators are able to monetise their influence by earning commissions on sales generated through their content.
In FY26, we enabled 63,213 Active Content Creators who generated over 1.4 million pieces of order-generating content on a cumulative basis. CEO Letter
Dear Shareholders,
Foundation of our Success

Foundation of our Success
For much of its history, e-commerce was built around a simple assumption: consumers knew what they wanted. They searched for it, compared options, and completed a transaction. That model worked well in markets where shopping was already organised around shopping aisles. Much of India, however, has traditionally shopped differently through recommendations: whether from a shopkeeper, a family member, a friend, or a local market. Meesho is built around this reality. Instead of requiring consumers to learn new behaviours, we use technology to make digital commerce feel more intuitive, more conversational and more aligned with how people already discover and evaluate products.
As we have grown, we have worked hard to preserve the principles that carried us through our hardest decisions. Our ‘Meesho Mantras’ are operating principles, not posters.
This year is close to my heart. It was our first year as a public listed company.
While much attention naturally goes to metrics such as users, orders, and NMV, I have always believed that numbers are outputs. The real work is the platform itself, and if the platform becomes more useful for consumers, more productive for sellers, more efficient for logistics partners , and more rewarding for creators, the numbers follow.

Our ‘User First’ mantra sends teams to spend time with consumers, sellers, and logistics partners before proposing solutions through programmes such as ‘Listen or Die’. ‘Problem First Mindset’ shapes how we organise: we build teams around the largest barriers our stakeholders face rather than around products or functions. Whether the challenge is improving trust, lowering the cost of trial, increasing relevance, or simplifying onboarding, the focus remains on solving the underlying problem rather than optimising individual functions.
By that measure, FY26 was one of our strongest years, and it was also a year in which we chose to invest heavily for the future. What began as a vision is now an identity. Meesho stands for something distinct in Indian e-commerce. We built a platform not only for those who were already online, but also for those who had never been. Our mission has always been simple: Democratise internet commerce for everyone.

This shift is important because it expands participation. Consumers who may not arrive with a specific purchase intent can still discover relevant products, while first- time online shoppers can navigate commerce through recommendations, content, and conversational experiences. As internet penetration increases and technology continues to reduce barriers around discovery, language, and trust, the addressable opportunity for e-commerce expands.
‘Lightspeed’, ‘Company over Team over Individual’, and ‘Extreme Ownership’ let small cross-functional pods own a problem end-to-end and decide close to the user, which is where most of our best work has come from. ‘Think Long Term’ governs how we allocate capital. Whether investing in technology, logistics capabilities, or user acquisition, we evaluate opportunities through the lens of long-term value creation rather than quarterly optics.

When people talk about the future of Indian e-commerce, the conversation often centres on market size. We think about it differently. The opportunity is not defined by how many people already use e-commerce. It is defined by how many barriers still remain between people and e-commerce. Those barriers take many forms. A consumer may not know how to navigate online shopping. A seller may not know how to start selling online. A logistics entrepreneur may not have the scale or know-how to participate in e-commerce networks. A creator may not have a way to monetise his creativity. Our experience over the last decade has reinforced a simple belief: the market expands in proportion to the barriers we remove.
The progress we made during FY26 reflects this.
Technology is what lets us remove barriers at scale, and increasingly it lets us remove ones we could not before.
Our endeavour is to find those barriers before anyone else does and to remove them quickly. We do that through two things: Culture and Technology.

Letter from CTO
Making Commerce Conversational
The Real Barrier to Commerce

The Real Barrier to Commerce
That belief led to Vaani, our voice AI shopping agent. What began as a small experiment quickly revealed something important: when users could interact with commerce in a way that felt natural, participation increased. More than 1.5 million consumers engaged with Vaani in its first month. Users who adopted the experience demonstrated meaningfully higher conversion rates, while many first- time shoppers who had previously abandoned the platform were able to complete purchases successfully.
When Vidit and I were working out what Meesho could be, the problem we cared about was making e-commerce accessible to people who had been historically left out.
Over the last decade, we have come to believe that the biggest barrier to participation in commerce is expertise and not access to the internet. Consumers have to know how to search, compare, and navigate digital platforms; sellers have to master cataloguing, pricing, and advertising; logistics providers are expected to build sophisticated operational networks and technology to deliver e-commerce parcels. Participation often requires learning systems that were never designed for most people.
Personalisation at Scale
The same idea extends far beyond voice.
Technology is changing that.

Technology is changing that.
For much of history, e-commerce rewarded expertise; now software is making it increasingly optional, shifting from giving tools to doing tasks for them.
Many consumers arrive not with a specific product in mind, but with a need, a budget, or simply curiosity. Legacy e-commerce assumes intent exists before discovery but in offline shopping in India, intent has always followed discovery. No two users are the same, so no two should see the same shopping aisle. As our understanding of users improves, the platform becomes increasingly personalised to the individual.
The implications are large. When participation becomes easier, more consumers transact online, more entrepreneurs start selling, more logistics providers join fulfillment networks, and more creators can monetise influence. The market grows because the barriers fall, not because the population changes.
Today, more than 75% of orders on Meesho originate from personalised feeds rather than search. PRISM (Personalised Ranking and Intent Signal Module), our recommendation system, combines long-term user preferences with real- time behavioural signals to help consumers discover products they may never have actively searched for.
Learning from Bharat
We saw this most clearly as we moved into smaller towns and rural India.

We saw this most clearly as we moved into smaller towns and rural India.
Many first-time internet users were not struggling with the products available on Meesho; what they struggled with was the interface.
We often watched users hesitate after opening the app - they knew what they wanted, but translating that into search queries and filters didn’t come naturally. Offline shopping is conversational: you describe what you need and get recommendations. Digital commerce instead expects users to learn an entirely new behaviour. We became convinced that e-commerce had to adapt to them, not the other way around.
Empowering Sellers through AI
The same shift is reaching sellers.
AI is increasingly powering core seller functions from cataloguing, pricing, advertising, and demand forecasting on their behalf. Through AI-powered cataloguing, demand intelligence, and GenAI voice agents, we are taking operational complexity off from sellers and allowing them to focus on their products rather than on platform mechanics. Lowering the expertise required to succeed online is one of the most powerful ways to expand participation in commerce.

This is the core difference between a platform and a linear business. In a linear business, serving twice the demand takes nearly twice the infrastructure - cost and capital rise with volume, so profitability doesn’t structurally improve with scale. In a platform business, each additional unit of demand costs less to serve, converting more growth into cash as it scales, true increasing returns to scale. Many businesses call themselves platforms, but few actually have these mechanics; most have digitised the customer experience while keeping a cost base that still scales with volume. Meesho is structurally one of the few in India that does, and that’s what underpins our confidence in long- term cash generation.

• Route Planning: Network Intelligence System (NIS), our ML-powered route planning system, optimizes truck allocation, route sequencing, and delivery timing simultaneously. NIS reduces cost per delivery by optimizing packet routing, continuously learns as network conditions evolve, and improves logistics efficiency as delivery volume grows.
• Address Intelligence: Geo-India LLM, our proprietary AI model trained on millions of real delivery traces across thousands of pin codes, encodes neighborhood connectivity the way a local delivery person understands it. For millions of first-time e-commerce users in India, addresses are landmarks, local references, and vernacular descriptions that conventional geocoding systems cannot parse. GeoIndia converts vernacular, landmark-based addresses into precise coordinates. Every corrected address feeds back into the model, compounding accuracy over time. In the last year, GeoIndia LLM improved geocoding accuracy by 20 percentage points and reduced misroute-related costs by 5 percent. Our research on GeoIndia LLM was published at CIKM 2025, where it outperformed industry standard commercial geo-coding systems across all evaluation metrics.

The opportunity
b. Deepen affordability and accessibility: Affordability is what converts first-time e-commerce users into habitual users. We will continue to make selling on Meesho affordable and accessible through technology- led operating efficiencies and continued optimisation of our platform. Lower seller costs and easy-operations translate into more competitive pricing and broader assortment in the low-ticket, high-frequency categories that define Bharat’s demand.

India’s e-commerce market is among the most under- penetrated of any large economy. It is sized at around 6 trillion (US$70 billion) in Gross Merchandise Value, just 7% of overall retail, against penetration of 34% in China, according to Redseer. This gap is a function of structural barriers in India’s e-commerce. India’s retail supply is deeply fragmented, with regional brands and unbranded products accounting for more than 70% of retail spends per Redseer, much of it sold by small sellers who have never come online. Layered on top are the barriers that keep first-time buyers offline altogether: limited trust in online transactions, language and literacy gaps, and the cost of e-commerce fulfillment in the country. The next wave of growth sits where these barriers are higher. E-commerce penetration in Tier 2+ cities is only around 4% in FY25 against roughly 14% in the top eight and Tier 1 cities as per Redseer. The same pattern holds by category. The first wave of Indian e-commerce was led by electronics, where penetration now nears 37%, while the categories that make up everyday Indian consumption remain barely online.

Over 70% of our code is now AI generated, and we are releasing products faster and with greater reliability than at any point in our history. c. Invest further in technology and AI: Technology is how we scale while keeping costs low. Through Meesho AI Labs we are building India-specific AI models for personalisation and product discovery, deploying agentic AI across the shopping and post-order journey, strengthening transaction risk management and improving advertising effectiveness for sellers. Alongside, we are building logistics and content-creator systems purpose-built for a low-cost environment, and expanding cloud infrastructure to handle higher volumes and peak demand. With the growing need to make e-commerce platforms more intuitive and assistive, helping customers discover the right choices, navigate products easily through best-in- class recommendation systems, and make purchases easier, Meesho has made significant developments across each of these phases.

At population scale with billions of product impressions, maintaining integrity through manual review is not economically viable. In FY2026, TrustMesh blocked c.9 Mn high-risk transactions, and restricted c.2 Mn consumers and c.62K sellers. Since deployment, TrustMesh has reduced RTO by >10%. This allows us to pursue initiatives that are scalable and strengthen our core business while driving long term value for our stakeholders and us.

A seller base of 55 to 60 million, still largely offline, is beginning to come online as onboarding and trust barriers ease. Making commerce affordable to buy and simple to access, in the consumer’s own language and at prices any Indian can pay, is what could turn India’s e-commerce under-penetration from a structural constraint into the largest consumption opportunity in retail.

3. STATE OF THE COMPANY’S AFFAIRS
Meesho is a multi-sided technology platform driving e-commerce in India by connecting four key stakeholders: consumers, sellers, logistics partners, and content creators. Our platform is designed to serve all segments of consumers across India by making e-commerce affordable, accessible and engaging. We are focused on providing ‘Everyday Low Prices’ to consumers enabled by our technology- first operations, platform scale and efficiency to offer low cost order fulfilment to sellers on Meesho. This, along with a zero commission model for sellers enables them to reduce the average cost charged to sellers and provide a wide assortment of products ranging from low cost unbranded products, regional brands and national brands at affordable prices on Meesho.

The Scheme was undertaken with the objective of streamlining and simplifying the corporate structure of the Company, including elimination of the cross-border management structure. Further, the segregation of the E-Commerce and Grocery businesses into separate entities was aimed at enabling focused management, independent growth and expansion opportunities, operational efficiencies, and optimum utilisation of resources. The Scheme was also intended to strengthen governance, enhance transparency and reporting standards, and provide greater flexibility for future fund-raising and strategic initiatives.

7. Policy for Determining Material Subsidiaries
In Fiscal 2026, Meesho’s proprietary logistics network, Valmo, delivered over 1,337 million orders through a robust ecosystem of 17,999 logistics partners and 1,19,860 delivery agents, forming the backbone of the Company’s marketplace operations. Meaning of Internal Financial Controls With Reference to Consolidated Financial Statements
A Company’s internal financial control with reference to consolidated financial statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of consolidated financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A Company’s internal financial control with reference to consolidated financial statements includes those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the Company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of consolidated financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the Company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the Company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the Company’s assets that could have a material effect on the consolidated financial statements.

Risk exposure
Gratuity is a defined benefit plan and the Group is expected to the following risks :
(a) Interest risk :
The plan exposes the Group to the risk of fall in interest rates. A fall in interest rates will result in an increase in the ultimate cost of providing the above benefit and will thus result in an increase in the value of the liability.

(b) Liquidity risk :

During the year ended March 31, 2025, the commercial courts have set aside the arbitral award. The Holding Company has appealed against the aforementioned judgement of commercial courts, before the Honorable High Court of Karnataka. This is the risk that the Group is not able to meet the short-term gratuity payouts. This may arise due to non availability of enough cash / cash equivalent to meet the liabilities.
(c) Salary escalation risk :
The present value of the defined benefit plan is calculated with the assumption of salary increase rate of plan participants in future. −Logistics business: It includes order fulfilment, which involves the entire process of managing products from the time an
order is placed until it is delivered to the end consumer. The logistics services cover order management, order pickup, transportation and timely delivery of goods to the end consumer. The Group manages logistics services through its logistics platform - ‘Valmo’ and third party logistics services providers. Until March 15, 2025, the Group charged order fulfillment fees from sellers and paid appropriate costs to the logistics partners for all stages of deliveries i.e. first mile, mid mile and last mile delivery services. Starting March 15, 2025, for orders fulfilled through Valmo (the technology of which is housed in the Holding Company), the Group began piloting a contractual model where certain last mile logistics partners provide services directly to sellers for order fulfillment fees, which are paid by sellers directly to logistics partners, for which the Group charges a platform facilitation fee to the logistics partner which is reported as part of Revenue from operations. For first mile and middle mile deliveries, the Group continued to collect order fulfilment fees from sellers and pay appropriate costs to logistics partners. During the year ended March 31, 2026, the aforesaid pilot was discontinued and the Group reverted to earlier model due to operational and comprehension challenges faced by the Sellers.

C Financial risk management

C Financial risk management
The Group is exposed to various financial risks majorly Credit risk, Liquidity risk and Market risk and equity price risk. The Holding Company’s Board of Directors has overall responsibility for the establishment and oversight of the Group’s risk management framework.
Expected credit loss (ECL) methodology
The Holding Company’s risk management policies are established to identify and analyse the risks faced by the Group, to set appropriate risk limits and controls and to monitor risks and adherence to limits. Risk management policies and systems are reviewed regularly to reflect changes in market conditions and the Group’s activities. The Group, through its training and management standards and procedures, aims to maintain a disciplined and constructive control environment in which all employees understand their roles and obligations.
The Group has assessed the credit risk associated with its financial guarantee contracts for provision of Expected Credit Loss (ECL) as at the reporting dates. The Group makes use of various reasonable supportive forward-looking parameters which are both qualitative as well as quantitative while determining the change in credit risk and the probability of default.
Inputs, assumptions and estimation techniques used to determine expected credit loss

Inputs, assumptions and estimation techniques used to determine expected credit loss
The Board of Directors of the Holding Company monitors compliance with the Group’s risk management policies and procedures, and reviews the adequacy of the risk management framework in relation to the risks faced by the Group.
The Group’s ECL provision are made on the basis of the Group’s historical loss experience and future expected credit loss, after factoring in various macro-economic parameter. In calculating the ECL, the management has considered internal and external information available up to the date of approval of these consolidated financial statements.
i. Credit risk
Credit risk is the risk that counterparty will not meet its obligations under a financial instrument or customer contract, leading to a financial loss. Financial instruments that are subject to credit risk and concentration thereof principally consist of (i) trade receivables, (ii) marketplace receivables and other financial assets, (iii) financial guarantee contracts and (iv) Investments, cash and cash equivalents and bank balances of the Group.

Interest rate risk is the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in market interest rates. The Group’s investments are predominantly held in mutual funds, bonds and bank deposits.
Credit risk on cash and cash equivalents and bank balances is limited as the group generally invests in deposits with banks and financial institutions with high credit ratings assigned by domestic credit rating agencies. e) Geographic concentration of credit risk
The Group also invests in mutual fund schemes of leading fund houses, such investments are susceptible to market interest risks which may impact the return and value of such investments. Liquidity risk is the risk that the Group will encounter difficulty in meeting the obligations associated with its financial liabilities that are settled by delivering cash or another financial asset. The Group’s approach to managing liquidity is to ensure, as far as possible, that it will have sufficient liquidity to meet its liabilities when they are due, under both normal and stressed conditions, without incurring unacceptable losses or risking damage to the Group’s reputation.

A company’s internal financial controls with reference to these standalone financial statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of standalone financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal financial control with reference to these standalone financial statements includes those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of standalone financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material effect on the standalone financial statements.

c) Common control business combinations

c) Common control business combinations
The Company’s Standalone Financial Statements were approved for issue in the meeting of the Company’s Board of Directors held on May 06, 2026.
Consequently, the subsidiaries of the erstwhile Holding Company viz., Meesho Payments Private Limited, India, Fashnear Shenzhen Trading Co. Ltd, China, PT Fashnear Technology Indonesia, Indonesia and Popshop Commerce Private Limited, India became the subsidiaries of the Company. The Company has accounted for the merger as a common control business combination as per the requirements of Appendix C to Ind AS 103 – Business Combinations read with the accounting treatment prescribed in the Composite Scheme. The said merger accounting has been given effect by restating comparative information in the Standalone Financial Statements for the year ended March 31, 2025 as if merger has taken place from the beginning of the earliest period presented.
Common control business combination refers to a business combination involving entities in which all the combining entities are ultimately controlled by the same party or parties both before and after the business combination, and that control is not transitory. Business combinations involving entities or businesses under common control have been accounted for using the pooling of interest method.

During the year ended March 31, 2025, the Board of Directors of the Company and its wholly owned subsidiaries Meesho Grocery Private Limited (‘MGPL’ or ‘Resultant Company-1’), Meesho Technologies Private Limited (‘MTPL’ or ‘Resultant Company-2’) and Meesho Inc. The assets and liabilities of the combining entities are reflected at their carrying amounts. No adjustments have been made to reflect fair values, or to recognise any new assets or liabilities. Adjustments are made only to harmonise accounting policies.
The estimates and underlying assumptions are reviewed on an ongoing basis. Revisions to accounting estimates are recognised in the year in which the estimate is revised if the revision affects only that year, or in the year of the revision and future years if the revision affects both current and future years.

The financial information in the Standalone Financial Statements in respect of prior period have been restated as if the business combination had occurred from the beginning of the earliest period presented in these Standalone Financial Statements, irrespective of the actual date of the combination. i. Current tax
Current tax assets and liabilities are measured at the amount expected to be recovered from or paid to the taxation authorities in accordance with the Income-tax Act, 1961 enacted in India. The tax rates and tax laws used to compute the amount are those that are enacted or substantively enacted, at the reporting date. Current income tax relating to items recognised outside the Standalone Statement of Profit and Loss is recognised outside the Standalone Statement of Profit and Loss (either in OCI or in equity in correlation to the underlying transaction). Management periodically evaluates whether it is probable that the relevant taxation authority would accept an uncertain tax treatment that the Company has used or plan to use in its income tax filings, including with respect to situations in which applicable tax regulations are subject to interpretation and establishes provisions, where appropriate. The Company shall reflect the effect of uncertainty for each uncertain tax treatment by using either most likely method or expected value method, depending on which method predicts better resolution of the treatment.

Deferred tax assets are recognised to the extent that it is probable that taxable profit will be available against which the deductible temporary differences, and the carry forward of unused tax credits and unused tax losses can be utilized. Unrecognised deferred tax assets are re-assessed at each reporting date and are recognised to the extent it has become probable that future taxable profits will allow the deferred tax asset to be recovered.

Provisions
A provision is recognised if, as a result of a past event, the Company has a present obligation that can be estimated reliably, and it is probable that an outflow of economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation. Provisions are recognised at the best estimate of the expenditure required to settle the present obligation at the reporting date. Impact of the New Labour Code:

Impact of the New Labour Code:
The Government of India w.e.f. November 21, 2025, notified the Code on Social Security, 2020, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (collectively referred to as the ‘Codes’), which replaces the existing central labour legislations. The Ministry of Labour & Employment published draft Central Rules and FAQs to enable assessment of the financial impact due to changes in regulations. Based on the Company’s assessment, the provisions currently in force do not have a material impact on these standalone financial statements. The Company continues to monitor the finalization of Central/State rules, notifications and clarifications from the Government on the other aspects of the Code.

During the year ended March 31, 2025, the Income Tax Authorities disputed certain allowances claimed by the company and made additions to the taxable income declared for AY 2022-23. During the year ended March 31, 2026, the Company filed a rectification request against the assessment order and has also filed a writ petition before the Honourable High Court of Karnataka. In the court hearing held on April 25, 2025, a stay order was issued for the aforesaid demand till the next date of hearing.

The Company’s risk management policies are established to identify and analyse the risks faced by the Company, to set appropriate risk limits and controls and to monitor risks and adherence to limits. Risk management policies and systems are reviewed regularly to reflect changes in market conditions and the Company’s activities. The Company, through its training and management standards and procedures, aims to maintain a disciplined and constructive control environment in which all employees understand their roles and obligations.
The carrying value of cash and cash equivalents, trade receivables, trade payables, other financial assets (including marketplace receivables), loan, certificate of deposits, Unit Linked Insurance Plan and other financial liabilities approximate to their fair values largely due to the short-term maturities of these instruments.

Credit risk is the risk that counterparty will not meet its obligations under a financial instrument or customer contract, leading to a financial loss. 3. To approve the alteration of the Articles of Association of the Company.
The Board of Directors of the Company, at its meeting held on July 23, 2026, approved the proposed amendments to Article 122 of the Articles of Association of the Company (‘Articles’), subject to the approval of the Members by way of a Special Resolution.
The proposed amendment to the Articles is being undertaken pursuant to the provisions of Sections 5 and 14 of the Companies Act, 2013 (the ‘Act’). Section 5 of the Act permits a company to include in its Articles provisions relating to the management of the Company, including provisions concerning the appointment of directors, while Section 14 enables a company to alter its Articles of Association by passing a Special Resolution.

The Company is currently in a high-growth phase within the competitive e-commerce marketplace sector. Our success to date has been anchored by the long-term vision of our Founders and the consistent support of our significant institutional investors. As the Company scales, the Board believes it is essential to ensure Institutional Continuity.
For the approval of right to nominate directors on the Board of the Company, Regulation 31B of the SEBI Listing Regulations, prescribes that any special right granted to the shareholders of a listed entity shall be subject to the approval by the shareholders in a General Meeting by way of a Special Resolution, to be obtained once in every five years starting from the date of grant of such special right.
Background and Context
Prior to the Company’s Initial Public Offering (‘IPO’), the composition and nomination rights of the Board of Directors were governed by the pre-IPO Shareholders’ Agreement (‘SHA’) and Part B of the Articles of the Company. Under the SHA, the Founders and certain major institutional investors held specific board nomination rights linked to their equity thresholds. To ensure compliance with public listing norms and facilitate a public-ready board structure, SHA and Part B of Articles, were terminated upon listing.

Accordingly, the approval of the Members is being sought for the proposed amendments to Article 122 of the Articles of Association of the Company. The Board believes that this institutionalized framework balances the protection of anchor investor rights with the highest standards of public market compliance, ensuring long-term corporate stability. Accordingly the Board recommends the Special Resolution set out at Item No. 3 of the Notice for approval by the Members.
Following the termination of the SHA, the Articles do not presently contain a comprehensive framework governing the continued participation of the founders on the Board or the nomination of directors by significant long-term institutional shareholders.
A copy of the existing Articles of the Company and the draft amended Articles proposed to be adopted pursuant to this Resolution shall be available for inspection by the Members at the Registered Office of the Company during business hours on all working days (except Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays) from the date of circulation of this Notice up to the date of the ensuing Annual General Meeting.
By formalizing board nomination rights for those with a significant economic interest, the Company ensures that its strategic direction remains aligned with its largest long-term stakeholders, preventing short-term volatility in leadership.

By formalizing board nomination rights for those with a significant economic interest, the Company ensures that its strategic direction remains aligned with its largest long-term stakeholders, preventing short-term volatility in leadership.
Strategic Rationale for the Proposed Framework
Mr. Vidit Aatrey (Promoter - Managing Director, Chairman & Chief Executive Officer) and Mr. Sanjeev Kumar (Promoter – Whole-time Director and Chief Technical Officer), being the Founders of the Company, are directly interested in this resolution to the extent that the proposed Article 122(a) formalises and codifies their right to continued Board representation, subject to maintaining the specified shareholding threshold.
As the Company enters its next phase of market expansion, the Board of Directors emphasizes the necessity of a stable, resilient, and predictable corporate governance architecture. To anchor the long-term corporate vision and insulate institutional decision-making from short-term market volatility, the Company proposes to amend its Articles to introduce a balanced, institutionalized Board Nomination Framework:

The Investor Nominee Directors presently on the Board, being nominees of Peak XV Partners Investments V and Elevation Capital V Limited, and their respective nominating Investors, are also interested in this resolution to the extent that the proposed Article 122(b) institutionalises and codifies the framework for Investor Nominee Directorships on the Board.
• Founders’ Nomination Framework: The Founders, Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Kumar, have been institutional to the Company’s growth trajectory. To ensure continuity of leadership, they shall be entitled to remain on and / or be appointed to the Board as long as they collectively hold at least 3.00% of the paid-up equity shares capital of the Company or 75,62,14,937 equity shares of the Company.
Save and except as stated above, none of the Directors or Key Managerial Personnel of the Company (as defined under the Act) and their immediate relatives are concerned or interested, financially or otherwise, except to the extent of their respective shareholding, if any, in the Company.

• Significant Investor Framework: To offer equitable, transparent rights to long-term institutional capital, a nomination right is being extended to the Top 2 largest non-promoter institutional investors holding at least 8.00% of the equity share capital of the company on a fully diluted basis. To protect minority interests and prevent an oversized board, this right is strictly capped at a maximum of two eligible institutional investors at any given point in time.

Moderator: Thank you so much, sir. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now begin with the question-and-answer
session. First question comes from the line of Vivek M with Jefferies. Please go ahead.
Vivek M: Hi, good evening, Meesho team. First, on the contribution margins this quarter 6% is a great
number. You have cautioned not to extrapolate this for the rest of the year. But from a second
half perspective, where do you think this number can -- should settle at? And also if you can
comment on FY28 as well?
Dhiresh Bansal: Sure. Thanks, Vivek, Dhiresh here. So, I think from a contribution margin perspective, the reason
why we mentioned that this is not to be assumed as going forward into the next quarter as well,
because typically we have certain lead lag between how we gain efficiencies on our cost front and
when do we kind of pass it back onto our sellers and hence consumers in the form of lower
pricing as well. So that's I think the key reason.
This quarter also, as we have kind of mentioned, we had incurred certain additional costs in
relation to servers, especially GPUs, and hence we did not kind of pass it along back. And as
that situation kind of normalizes, we would kind of reduce pricing to fund further growth into
Page 2 of 15
Meesho Limited October 28, 2026
our flywheel.
From a full-year perspective, we don't give specific guidance. Of course, I think we will continue

chunks.section: Nov 2026 earnings call · Q2 FY2027 · Questions and answers

From a full-year perspective, we don't give specific guidance. Of course, I think we will continue
to make progress on the longer-term contribution margin targets that we have during the course
of this year. So it will be substantially better than FY26, both with kind of the efficiencies that
we are gaining on the logistics side and hence what we have there and also kind of moving into
FY28, we will start seeing benefits coming in from ad monetization as percentage of NMV
increasing.
Vivek M: Got it, Dhiresh. The second one is on the -- and in some ways related to CMs. Logistics
efficiency, you have spoken about 15% faster deliveries. So, two parts. One is on a Y-o-Y basis
because festive season is in different quarter.
Is there also a network effect or underutilization, let's say, so to speak in some ways this year
versus last year, which is helping this 15%? And again, this 15% should be seen for 2Q plus 3Q
combined? And the second part is, if you can just comment on Valmo, how things have been
there on that front?
Dhiresh Bansal: Sure. So the first part of the question in respect to the speed improvement that we have seen in
this quarter, that's a continuing trend. So even in Q2 and Q3 put together, we expect that to kind
of continue. The reason why that is happening, I think we have mentioned a few, but just to

chunks.section: Nov 2026 earnings call · Q2 FY2027 · Questions and answers
chunks.text:
of continue. The reason why that is happening, I think we have mentioned a few, but just to
highlight, one, the fact that density increase and especially as we kind of have more capacity
creation that has happened across the course of the year, that also kind of helps with faster
delivery timelines.
So to give you an instance, let's say on the same route, earlier we were operating two shifts, now
we are able to operate three shifts of line haul, then the speed would improve. So the growth
itself and the density kind of leads to better speed across the network. We have also aided that
with kind of better network design that has happened across our network and some of the 3PL
networks as well.
And lastly, I think improvements on the software side, which is GeoIndia LLM, which is a more
sustainable improvement that we keep doing in the form of improvement of address accuracy,
hence making it easier to find end users has been the reason for improvement in speed. So that
we expect to sustain across the quarters too.
Vivek M: And Dhiresh, comments on Valmo?
Dhiresh Bansal: Yes, so I think we continue to make progress on Valmo in terms of reducing our cost of doing
business and I think even from a capacity perspective, we have had a good festive season. So
some of the problems, let's say, that the overall logistics ecosystem saw last year, I think they

some of the problems, let's say, that the overall logistics ecosystem saw last year, I think they
are largely kind of behind us and this festive season has been good both in terms of capacity
availability as well as efficiency of the operations. So that's I think on the Valmo as well as
overall logistics side.
Vivek M: Got it. And if I can ask, one more which is on the outlook side, you have mentioned about you
are watchful on the micro side, while you stand for value, but there is a fair amount of discretion,

I am guessing at the value level also for the kind of users you serve.
How worried are you with the macro and does that worry you from a let's say 12-month
perspective? I know world is very volatile, there are a lot of uncertainties, but can the household
budgets, can that impact the point that you made? Basically how worried are you about it?
Vidit Aatrey: Yes, hi Vivek, this is Vidit here. On this particular point, actually, from whatever data we have
seen on the user behaviour, we do not see any concern yet. We see like now a large part of our
platform is about utility products, personal care, beauty, home, kitchen, baby care, a lot of this
is stuff that people need and we help them people save money. So we see like healthy amount of
traffic conversion on our platform. So we do not see like any concern emerging anywhere.

chunks.section: Nov 2026 earnings call · Q2 FY2027 · Questions and answers

traffic conversion on our platform. So we do not see like any concern emerging anywhere.
Like a large part of the thing that we have highlighted is we continue to see like supply chain
disruptions on the seller side. Like a lot of our sellers, because the price have been volatile, it
impacts supply chains. We have been trying to help them out as much as we can, but last one
month also, there were a lot of disruptions that happened because of price changing of crude
across the board and a lot of petroleum products are used in supply chains from our sellers across
categories and products.
So we see like a lot of pain point on the seller side, but on the demand side, actually, we haven't
seen and we believe because we stand for value and especially in times where the macro could
be impacted, we as a platform will add a lot more value to consumers' lives. So on the demand
side, we actually feel quite confident that things should be okay.

Moderator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Navin Killa with UBS. Please go ahead.
Navin Killa: Hi, thanks for the opportunity. I had two questions actually. So, you did mention on the logistics
side about improvement in delivery timings and all. I suppose there is always a cost versus speed
trade-off. So, how do you see these two kind of factors playing out over the course of the next
two to three years?
And then secondly, the financial services and the BNPL and the fintech products, if there is any
kind of information or data that you can share and ambitions on, how big the business could be
given, some very interesting precedents in in other emerging markets. So, how do you see that
opportunity?
Vidit Aatrey: Yes, I think on the first question, maybe I can take that on logistics cost versus speed
improvement. The way we see it is not as a trade-off. So, whenever we do speed improvements,
we hold the cost and then kind of make those speed improvements. The reason why they happen,
like I mentioned, for instance, if density of the network increases, that leads to faster speed. It
also comes with better cost actually.
So, they both move in the same direction when it comes to things like density. When it is about
let's say using GeoIndia LLM uh for improving accuracy of address, both cost improve because

the number of attempts required to deliver a product comes down and also the speed improves

not deteriorating cost, how can we keep improving speed?
And as the volumes grow, there is natural benefit that we get, which we further aid by improving
our network design as well as, software improvements like GeoIndia LLM. So, we do not see

is no, because a lot of this is flywheel-related impact. Whenever we reduce our pricing, products
and categories that were unviable last year or last month start to become viable, sellers in that
category get attracted to the platform, start selling, and the payoff happens over a long time
period. Right?
So a lot of these changes do not lead to a massive bump in the short term, but we have leading
indicators to see how it will impact our two quarters, three quarters, four quarters down the line.

Key takeaways
● Annual Transacting Users grew 29% YoY to 274 million; LTM frequency improved to 10.3 as earlier cohorts deepened engagement. ● Annual Transacting Sellers grew by 81% YoY to 1.04 million sellers particularly through acquiring MSME sellers through targeted campaigns and improved word-of-mouth referrals. This was further supported by seller success initiatives such as AI-powered cataloguing, demand intelligence, Gen AI voice agents supporting local languages, and product improvements that help new sellers gain visibility faster on the platform. ● Placed Orders grew 29% YoY to 725 million in Q1 FY27, while NMV increased 34% YoY to ₹11,614 Cr, supported by sustained new user onboarding and deeper engagement from existing users. NMV growth outpaced order growth for the quarter supported by lower Cancellations and Return-to-Origin (RTO) rates due to enhancements to ‘TrustMesh’ algorithms filtering out high-risk orders. ● Contribution Margin expanded to 4.6% in Q1 FY27, supported by continued logistics cost efficiencies, and improved platform monetization. Last Twelve Months (LTM) Free Cash Flow stood at (₹537) crores and LTM Free Cash Flow to Equity stood at (₹164) crores; with cash balance of ₹6,521 crores. ● We made significant progress this quarter towards an autonomous SDLC. We shifted code authorship, testing, and documentation to AI agents, while enabling engineers to focus on specifications, reviews, and outcomes. This has already delivered more than 2x productivity gains across our engineering organization.

Investments in technology to enhance accessibility

Investments in technology to enhance accessibility
● As part of our broader AI-led productivity agenda, we launched AI Blitz, an internal initiative to systematically embed AI agents into our engineering workflows. This has resulted in 2x+ productivity gains across the board, varying by task type. This is a long term investment and central to this is an autonomous Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC), built around a clear division of responsibility. AI agents now author code, tests, and documentation, while engineers focus on writing specs, reviewing output, and owning outcomes. Built-in feedback loops and enforcement guardrails, ensures these gains compound over time without regression, positioning us for continuous improvement in engineering efficacy going forward. As this scales, engineering bandwidth becomes less of a constraint on how fast we can build, giving us structural operating leverage as the business grows.
Adjusted EBITDA - New Initiatives

Adjusted EBITDA - New Initiatives
Adjusted EBITDA for new initiatives including Financial Services, our Low-Cost Logistics Network came in at (₹39) crores for Q1 FY27. These are what we call our Horizon2 (H2) portfolio: Early stage bets that sit outside the core marketplace, with their own budget and their own economics. The core business does not depend on any of them. What the portfolio buys us is a shot at building the next big business, at a cost that is capped and known in advance.
This approach has worked before. Valmo and Content Commerce both started as H2 experiments and are now core parts of the platform. This quarter we added one more bet with the Kirana Club acquisition (which is slated to close in Q2FY27).
Total burn across all H2 initiatives has a hard budget cap. An initiative stays experimental until it shows real adoption and retention post which it graduates to H1, where further growth capital is allocated based on the same investment framework applied as the rest of the platform.
Empowering India’s Entrepreneurs

Empowering India’s Entrepreneurs
The platform now serves over 1.04 million seller entrepreneurs, up 81% YoY, with MSME sellers joining through targeted campaigns and, increasingly, word of mouth. Our seller growth is most pronounced beyond India's largest cities: Tier 4 sellers grew 125% YoY, outpacing every other tier, and sellers from Tier 2 towns and beyond now make up 45% of our total base. This underserved geography remains largely untapped by e-commerce more broadly, and it is where our seller network is scaling fastest.
Part of what makes this possible is that selling on Meesho no longer demands technical fluency or English proficiency. AI-powered cataloguing, demand intelligence, and GenAI voice agents that work in local languages have brought down the effort it takes to launch and run a business on the platform.

This quarter, we extended the same mission to a second cohort of entrepreneurs - India’s retailers esp. kirana store owners through our recently announced acquisition of Kirana Club, a 3P marketplace connecting FMCG brands and distributors with retailers across Tier 2+ and rural India, a segment existing B2B platforms have largely left unserved. The ambition is to build 'Meesho for Retailers' as the lowest-cost, most accessible channel for a kirana store to source from any brand or manufacturer. We continue to see significant opportunities to strengthen access, transparency, and product discovery for kirana stores in underserved markets across India, and to extend this approach to B2B retail more broadly.
Outlook and final thoughts

Outlook and final thoughts
We continue to remain watchful of the macro environment. Crude prices have moderated this quarter, and Indian retail fuel prices have stayed largely unchanged since the end of May. Combined with our ongoing efficiency initiatives and scale benefits, the direct impact on our business remains limited, and we have not seen meaningful price increases on the platform.
Looking to Q2 FY27, we want to set expectations on two counts.
First, on growth spends: Q1 was a seasonally soft quarter, and spends were held lower at ~2.1% of NMV. With the festive season approaching, we will step up new-user acquisition meaningfully from Q2 onwards. Every rupee of this goes through the same capital allocation and investment frameworks that govern all our investments. Marketing is a cost we incur upfront to onboard new users to our platform; the users it brings compound in value over quarters and years. We spend when the return case is strongest, and the festive build-up is exactly that window.

Second, on NMV growth optics: Our flagship sale event (Meesho Mega Blockbuster Sale) moves to Q3 this year, from Q2 last year. Q2 YoY comparisons will therefore look softer than underlying trend; while Q3 will look better. The reason is purely timing, and not change in underlying momentum. Last year’s Q2 included the sale; while this year’s Q2 will not. We expect the comparison to normalise if we consider Q2 and Q3 together.
Taken together: Q2 will show higher user growth spend and slower NMV growth, both by design and shift in festive seasonality this year. We are comfortable trading one quarter's optics for a stronger festive season on a compounding platform. Every additional consumer, seller and data point makes the future growth more durable.
That concludes our update for this quarter. We thank our shareholders, as always, for their continued confidence in our long-term vision.
